blocks.text: I can use the reflexive pronoun ‘se’ before a range of verbs in the context of describing the Mexican custom ‘Day of the Dead’.
I can accurately pronounce words with penultimate syllable stress.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like ‘myself’ and ‘yourself’
word that goes before a noun to show ownership or belonging
possessive adjective ‘his’, ‘her’ or ‘its’ for singular nouns
possessive adjective ‘his’, ‘her’ or ‘its’ for plural nouns

blocks.text: Penultimate means ‘second-last’. Say these words aloud: the stress is on the second-last syllable.

items: vamos
sobre
mundo
amigo
playa
problema
barrio
tienen
casa
coches

blocks.text: In Spanish, words ending in a {vowel}, {-n} or {-s} generally have penultimate syllable stress. No accent is needed.
When a word only has two syllables, the second-last is actually the first, as in **playa** and **barrio**.
If a word ending in a **different consonant** has penultimate syllable stress, there is an accent on the stressed vowel.

items: f{ú}tbol
dif{í}cil
{ú}til
{á}rbol
l{á}piz
d{é}bil

blocks.label: What about flores?
blocks.text: ‘Lápiz’ ends in -z and ‘débil’ in -l, so they both need an accent to show the penultimate syllable stress. ‘Flores’ ends in -s, so it doesn’t!

blocks.q: All of these words have penultimate syllable stress. Which column does each word belong in?
columns: No accent needed (ends in a vowel, -n or -s)
Accent needed (ends in a different consonant)

blocks.text: These verbs are all in Nadia’s story. Some end in -se: that is the reflexive pronoun ‘se’ joined to the verb.

blocks.q: Match each Spanish verb to its English meaning.

blocks.text: Some Spanish verbs have a **completely different meaning** when used with a reflexive pronoun.

items: quedar = to meet up: queda con amigos (she, he meets up with friends)
quedarse = to remain, to stay: se queda en casa (she, he stays at home)
acordar = to agree on: acuerda el precio (she, he agrees on the price)
acordarse = to remember: se acuerda (she, he remembers)

blocks.text: Reflexive verbs are not just for routine activities: there are many reflexive verbs in Spanish.

blocks.q: Choose the correct meaning of each sentence.

options: She meets up with her friends.

blocks.text: **Acordarse** has a stem change from o to ue in the forms for ‘I’, ‘you (singular)’, ‘she, he, it’ and ‘they’.

items: yo me ac{ue}rdo — I remember
tú te ac{ue}rdas — you remember
ella, él se ac{ue}rda — she, he, it remembers
ellos, ellas se ac{ue}rdan — they remember

blocks.text: **Sentarse** has a stem change from e to ie in the same forms.

items: yo me s{ie}nto — I sit down
tú te s{ie}ntas — you sit down
ella, él se s{ie}nta — she, he, it sits down
ellos, ellas se s{ie}ntan — they sit down

blocks.text: When the ‘doer’ and the ‘receiver’ of the verb are **not** the same person, we use an **a** before the object.

items: Lava al perro. (She, he washes the dog.)
Sienta al niño cerca. (She, he sits the child down nearby.)

blocks.text: When the ‘doer’ and the ‘receiver’ are the **same person**, we use a reflexive pronoun before the verb. **Se** means ‘himself’, ‘herself’ or ‘itself’.

items: Se lava. (She, he washes herself, himself.)
Se sienta cerca. (She, he sits herself, himself down nearby.)

blocks.text: In English, the reflexive pronouns are sometimes optional, but never in Spanish!

blocks.q: Which sentence means ‘She washes the dog’?
blocks.why: The doer (she) and the receiver (the dog) are different, so there is no reflexive pronoun, and we use a before the object.
The doer and the receiver are the same person, so we use the reflexive pronoun se.

blocks.q: Which sentence means ‘She sits the child down nearby’?
blocks.why: The doer (she) and the receiver (the child) are different, so we use a before the object and no reflexive pronoun.

blocks.text: **Su** (‘his’, ‘her’, ‘its’) and **se** (‘herself’, ‘himself’, ‘itself’) are similar, so take care! Su(s) goes before a noun. Se goes before a verb.

blocks.q: Choose se, su or sus to complete each sentence.

items.q: ___ abuelos son simpáticos. (Her grandparents are kind.)
Nadia ___ sienta al lado de su abuela. (Nadia sits down next to her grandmother.)
Nadia va a la calle con ___ hermano. (Nadia goes to the street with her brother.)

blocks.text: Nadia has Mexican family and tells Lucía about Día de Muertos, a very well-known Mexican tradition.

items: Día de Muertos is a unique custom, and very important for the Mexican community.
It is a way of thinking about the dead.
For Mexicans, the dead come to the Earth on this day.
‘Pan de muerto’ is a type of traditional bread.

blocks.text: An altar is a type of table used for religious ceremonies or spiritual offerings.
In the morning, Nadia gets up early to help her grandmother. They prepare pan de muerto and a little fruit for the altar. Her altar has various levels.
Nadia puts photos of her grandfather there and sits down next to her grandmother. She stays at home for a few hours with her family and remembers her grandfather.
In the afternoon, she puts on fun clothes, paints herself white and black and goes to the street with her brother. In her neighbourhood there is a festival with loud music and coloured lights.

blocks.q: What is the first level of Nadia’s altar?
blocks.why: The levels of the altar are different parts of the world: the first level is the Earth and the second is the sky.

blocks.q: What do Nadia and her grandmother prepare for the altar?
options: Pan de muerto and a little fruit
blocks.why: They prepare pan de muerto and a little fruit for the altar.

blocks.q: ‘Nadia se pinta de blanco y negro.’ What does it mean?
options: Nadia paints herself white and black.
Nadia paints her house white and black.
blocks.why: Se pinta has the reflexive pronoun se: Nadia does it to herself.

items: Spanish words ending in a vowel, -n or -s naturally have penultimate syllable stress, e.g. vamos and mundo.
If a word ending in a different consonant has penultimate syllable stress, there is an accent on the stressed vowel, e.g. fútbol.
Some Spanish verbs have a completely different meaning when used with a reflexive pronoun, e.g. quedar (to meet up) and quedarse (to stay, remain).
The reflexive pronoun se means ‘himself’, ‘herself’ or ‘itself’ before a verb, e.g. se lava.
To say ‘his’, ‘her’ or ‘its’ before a noun we use su (singular) or sus (plural).

flashcards.front: Which words naturally have penultimate (second-last) syllable stress?
flashcards.back:
Words ending in a vowel, -n or -s.

vamos, mundo

flashcards.front: When does a word with penultimate syllable stress need an accent?
flashcards.back:
When it ends in a different consonant: the accent goes on the stressed vowel.

fútbol, difícil, útil, árbol
No. It ends in -s, so penultimate stress is natural.

to meet up

Queda con amigos.

to remain, to stay

Se queda en casa.

to agree on

Acuerda el precio.

o to ue

me acuerdo, te acuerdas, se acuerda, se acuerdan

e to ie

me siento, te sientas, se sienta, se sientan

flashcards.front: What does the reflexive pronoun “se” mean?
flashcards.back:
himself, herself or itself

Se lava. (She, he washes herself, himself.)

flashcards.front: What is the difference between “Lava al perro” and “Se lava”?
flashcards.back:
Lava al perro = She, he washes the dog (doer and receiver are different, so we use a).
Se lava = She, he washes herself, himself.

flashcards.front: How do you say “his, her or its” before a plural noun?
What is the difference between “se” and “su”?
flashcards.back:
Se goes before a verb (se sienta).
Su goes before a noun (su familia).

flashcards.front: In Nadia’s altar, what is the first level and what is the second?
flashcards.back: The first level is the Earth (la Tierra) and the second level is the sky (el cielo).

worksheet.title: Worksheet: A Mexican tradition: reflexive pronoun ‘se’
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a short answer. Some answers are in Spanish and some are in English. Use the rules for stress, the meanings of the verbs, and se and su from the lesson.

questions.prompt: The word “lapiz” has penultimate syllable stress and ends in -z. Write it with its accent.
questions.explanation: A word ending in a consonant other than -n or -s with penultimate syllable stress has an accent on the stressed vowel.

questions.prompt: The word “debil” has penultimate syllable stress and ends in -l. Write it with its accent.
questions.explanation: It ends in a different consonant (-l), so the accent goes on the stressed vowel.

questions.prompt: Does the word “flores” need an accent? Answer yes or no.
questions.explanation: It ends in -s, so penultimate syllable stress is natural and no accent is needed.

questions.prompt: “Queda con sus primos.” Complete the English: “She ___ up with some cousins.” (one word)
“Se queda en casa por la mañana.” Complete the English: “She ___ at home in the morning.” (one word)
questions.explanation: Quedarse means to remain, to stay.

questions.prompt: “Acuerda la hora de la fiesta.” Complete the English: “She ___ on the time of the party.” (one word)
“Se acuerda de personas especiales.” Complete the English: “She ___ special people.” (one word)
Write se or su: … queda en la cocina para organizar la comida. (She stays in the kitchen to organise the food.)
questions.explanation: Queda is a verb, and Nadia does it herself, so we need se.

questions.prompt: Write se or su: … familia prepara un altar con papeles de colores y luces. (Her family prepares an altar with coloured paper and lights.)
questions.explanation: Familia is a noun, so we need su (‘her’).

questions.prompt: Write se or su: … casa está llena de flores. (Her house is full of flowers.)
questions.explanation: Casa is a noun, so we need su (‘her’).

questions.prompt: Write se or su: … sienta en la habitación para ver las fotos. (She sits down in the room to see the photos.)
questions.explanation: Sienta is a verb, and she sits herself down, so we need se.

questions.prompt: Write se or su: … hermano participa en el festival. (Her brother participates in the festival.)
questions.explanation: Hermano is a noun, so we need su (‘her’).
